clinicalPearls: A leading monogenic cause of auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder, inherited in an autosomal recessive manner through biallelic OTOF variants
Typically presents as congenital severe-to-profound hearing loss with preserved otoacoustic emissions and absent auditory brainstem responses
The defect is presynaptic (a cochlear synaptopathy), so the auditory nerve is intact and can be stimulated directly
Cochlear implantation generally produces excellent auditory and speech outcomes
A rare temperature-sensitive variant causes marked hearing deterioration during fever with recovery afterwards
Outer hair cell function may be preserved early, so emissions can be present in infancy and disappear over time
OTOF is a prominent target for emerging inner-ear gene-replacement approaches, making molecular confirmation increasingly relevant
reference.pathophysiology: Otoferlin is a calcium-sensing protein essential for synaptic vesicle exocytosis at the inner hair cell ribbon synapse. When OTOF variants impair its function, the influx of calcium fails to trigger reliable neurotransmitter release onto the auditory nerve terminals, so sound is transduced by hair cells but not faithfully relayed to the nerve. This presynaptic synaptopathy underlies the characteristic pattern of preserved outer hair cell responses with an absent or grossly dyssynchronous brainstem response. Because the spiral ganglion neurones and auditory nerve remain structurally intact, direct electrical stimulation by a cochlear implant bypasses the defective synapse effectively.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic and acquired causes of auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder
Neural auditory neuropathy from spiral ganglion or nerve pathology
additionalInvestigations: Otoacoustic emissions and cochlear microphonic recording showing preserved outer hair cell activity
Auditory brainstem response demonstrating absence or gross dyssynchrony
Behavioural and speech perception audiometry as age allows
Targeted OTOF sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis within a deafness panel
Cross-sectional imaging to confirm an intact cochlear nerve before implantation
Temperature-dependent threshold assessment when febrile fluctuation is reported
redFlags: Profound functional deficit and language delay despite a deceptively preserved emission profile
Marked hearing deterioration during febrile illness in the temperature-sensitive form
Loss of previously present emissions over time
Missed diagnosis when newborn screening relies on emissions alone
reference.prognosis: Because the lesion is presynaptic with an intact nerve, cochlear implantation typically restores excellent speech perception, and molecular confirmation may open access to gene-based therapies as they mature.
pitfalls: Interpreting present otoacoustic emissions as normal hearing and delaying intervention
Attributing febrile hearing fluctuation to middle-ear disease rather than the temperature-sensitive phenotype
Trialling prolonged amplification when implantation is more appropriate
Not confirming an intact cochlear nerve on imaging before planning an implant
